cases.input: Teach me Cramer’s rule; I know basic algebra.
cases.response:
Our target is to solve a 2×2 system, check the answer, and recognize when Cramer’s rule cannot give a unique solution. We’ll do determinants → one example → your independent solution → a singular-system check.

For a matrix with rows (a,b) and (c,d), its determinant is ad−bc. First check: what is the determinant of rows (3,1) and (2,4)?

Cramer’s rule applies when the coefficient determinant D is nonzero. Replace the x column with the right-hand constants to get Dx; replace the y column to get Dy. Then x=Dx/D and y=Dy/D.

Example: 2x+y=7, x−y=2.
D=2(−1)−1(1)=−3.
Dx=7(−1)−1(2)=−9.
Dy=2(2)−7(1)=−3.
Thus x=3, y=1. Check: 6+1=7 and 3−1=2.

Now solve x+2y=8, 3x−y=3. Show all three determinants and substitute your answer into both equations. We’ll advance when your column replacements, signs, and explanation agree; if a step fails, we’ll isolate it. Later, try a fresh problem without the formula visible and explain what D=0 leaves undecided.

[OpenStax](https://openstax.org/books/college-algebra-2e/pages/7-8-solving-systems-with-cramers-rule) supplies the algebra reference; [IES](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/PracticeGuide/1) supports alternating examples and attempts. Both inspected today. Nothing saved for this short lesson.

cases.input: The determinant is zero for x+y=2, 2x+2y=4. So no solution? What about x+y=2, 2x+2y=5?
cases.response:
D=0 means the system has no unique solution. It does not distinguish no solutions from infinitely many.

In the first system, doubling x+y=2 gives exactly 2x+2y=4. Both equations describe the same line. Every pair (t,2−t) works, so there are infinitely many solutions.

In the second, doubling the first equation still gives 2x+2y=4, while the other equation demands 2x+2y=5. Subtraction gives 0=1: a contradiction, so there are no solutions.

Your determinant calculation is useful; the conclusion needs an extra consistency check. Cramer’s quotients require D≠0. When D=0, switch to elimination or substitution. [OpenStax’s Cramer’s rule section](https://openstax.org/books/college-algebra-2e/pages/7-8-solving-systems-with-cramers-rule), inspected in this execution, states the nonzero requirement.

Try transferring the distinction: compare x−2y=3 with (a) 3x−6y=9 and (b) 3x−6y=8. Classify each and show the equation obtained by elimination. A correct classification plus the identity or contradiction will establish this distinction for these examples; it won’t yet establish general mastery. No progress file has been saved.

cases.input: I have not stated how much time I have. Teach me fractions.
cases.response:
Your available time is unknown, so I’ll start with a compact lesson without assigning a daily schedule. Our target is to explain, compare, and combine fractions using equal-sized parts.

Sequence: what the parts mean → equivalent fractions and comparison → addition/subtraction with common units → a recipe or measurement problem. We’ll advance when you can explain the units and solve a new example, then try a fresh application later.

A fraction such as 3/4 means three pieces when one whole is divided into four equal pieces. The denominator tells the size of the parts; the numerator counts them. The same whole can be divided into eight equal pieces: each quarter becomes two eighths, so 3/4=6/8.

A useful boundary: three slices out of four unequal slices needn’t be 3/4 of the pizza. Equal parts and the same whole matter.

Try drawing one rectangle divided into four equal parts and shading three. Divide each part in half. What fraction is shaded now, and why did the amount stay unchanged? Next, compare 1/2 and 3/8 using a common whole.

[OpenStax’s fractions section](https://openstax.org/books/prealgebra-2e/pages/4-1-visualize-fractions), inspected today, supports this concrete-to-symbolic start. Nothing saved; your explanation will determine the next step.
